title: The physics of sport: how the ground, a throw and a kick change how things move

summary.text: Drop a ball on a stone floor and it bounces back up. Drop the same ball on a pillow and it hardly moves again. A bounce needs something to squash and spring back fast. On a hard floor the ball does that. On a pillow, the pillow squashes instead and springs back too slowly to push the ball. The same is true for a runner, so running on soft sand is tiring work. A thrown ball keeps moving forward while gravity pulls it down, so it flies in a curve. A kick off the middle of a ball makes it spin, and a spinning ball curves in the air. In every sport, the player, the ball and the ground push on each other.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a tennis ball bouncing high off a stone floor, on the right the same ball sinking into a white pillow, and behind them a girl running on a beach and another girl throwing a ball in a long curve.

intro.hook: Try this. Hold a ball at the height of your chin and let it fall onto the floor. Catch it. Now let it fall onto a pillow. It is the same ball, falling from the same height. Why does it bounce back up from the floor, but hardly at all from the pillow?
intro.text: Every game you play is full of questions like this. Why is it so tiring to run on the beach? Why does a ball you throw fly in a curve, and not in a straight line? How do footballers make a ball bend in the air? In this unit you test bounces on different floors in your own home. You find out what the ground does to a ball, and to your feet. Then you look at throwing, kicking, jumping and catching.
intro.art: A child's hand letting go of a tennis ball above a tiled floor, and next to it the same ball sitting in a dent in a pillow.

outcomes: I can explain that a ball bounces because it squashes and springs back, and that a soft surface squashes instead and gives the bounce back slowly.
I can run a fair test of how high one ball bounces on different surfaces, and show my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can explain why running on soft sand takes more work than running on a hard road, and how my legs act like springs.
I can explain why a thrown ball flies in a curve, and that a faster ball goes further before it lands.
I can explain how a kick off the middle of a ball makes it spin, and that a spinning ball curves in the air.
I can explain how swinging my arms helps me jump further, and how soft hands make a catch gentler.
I can tell the story of how Tartaglia and Galileo found the true path of a thrown ball.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. A force can start something moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, turn it or change its shape.
terms.example: When you kick a ball, your foot pushes it. That push is a force.
terms.art: A foot kicking a football, with an arrow showing the push.

terms.meaning: When a moving thing hits a surface and moves back off it.
terms.example: A tennis ball dropped on a tiled floor bounces back up about half the height it fell from.
terms.art: A tennis ball with dotted arcs showing it bouncing three times, each bounce lower.

terms.meaning: The top or outside layer of something, the part that is touched.
terms.example: A tiled floor, a doormat and a pillow are three different surfaces.
terms.art: Three squares side by side: grey tiles, a rough doormat and a soft pillow.

terms.meaning: Able to spring back to its old shape after it is squashed or stretched.
terms.example: A rubber ball is elastic. Squeeze it and let go, and it is round again at once.
terms.art: A hand squeezing a rubber ball flat, and the ball round again next to it.

terms.meaning: What something needs to move, warm up or make a sound. Energy is never used up. It changes from one kind to another.
terms.example: A falling ball has energy of movement. When it hits a pillow, most of that energy turns into a little warmth and sound.
terms.art: A ball falling into a pillow, with tiny wavy lines rising from the pillow.

terms.meaning: The pull of the Earth on everything. It pulls things down towards the ground.
terms.example: Gravity pulls a thrown ball down, so it always comes back to the ground.
terms.art: A ball in the air with an arrow pointing down towards the Earth.

terms.meaning: The grip between two things that touch. It acts against sliding.
terms.example: Friction between your feet and the floor lets you push off when you run.
terms.art: A bare foot pushing back on a floor, with a small arrow for friction pointing forward.

terms.meaning: How high a ball goes back up after it bounces.
terms.example: Kavya dropped her ball from 100 cm. It went back up to 55 cm, so the rebound height was 55 cm.
terms.art: A wall with a paper ruler, a ball at the top of a bounce, and a dotted line from the ball to the 55 cm mark.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same.
terms.example: To test floors, use the same ball and drop it from the same height each time. Change only the floor.
terms.art: The same ball above three different floors, with the same height mark above each.

terms.meaning: The line a thrown thing follows through the air. It goes up, bends over, and comes down. Scientists call this curve a parabola.
terms.example: A cricket ball thrown from the boundary flies in a curved path to the wicket keeper.
terms.art: A dotted curve from a girl's hand, rising and falling to another girl's hands.

terms.meaning: How much something is turned or tilted. Angles are measured in degrees.
terms.example: Throwing a ball straight up is an angle of 90 degrees. Throwing it flat along the ground is 0 degrees.
terms.art: Three arrows from one hand: flat, halfway up, and straight up, with their angles written beside them.

terms.meaning: Turning round and round while moving.
terms.example: A kick on the side of a football makes it spin as it flies.
terms.art: A football in the air with curved arrows around it showing it turning.

terms.meaning: A strong, stretchy cord that joins a muscle to a bone. Tendons stretch and spring back like rubber bands.
terms.example: The Achilles tendon at the back of your heel stretches each time your foot lands when you run.
terms.art: A drawing of a leg from the side, with the Achilles tendon at the back of the heel coloured in.

terms.meaning: The push of the air against something moving through it. It slows things down.
terms.example: A crumpled paper ball and a flat sheet of paper fall differently because of air resistance.
terms.art: A paper ball falling straight and a flat sheet of paper drifting, with small arrows of air pushing up.

explanations.definition: A ball bounces when it squashes against a surface and then springs back to its round shape. As it springs back, it pushes on the surface, and the surface pushes it back up.
explanations.description: When a falling ball hits a hard floor, it stops for a tiny moment. In that moment it squashes flat at the bottom. A rubber ball is elastic, so it springs back to round almost at once. That springing back pushes on the floor, and the floor pushes the ball up. All this happens in a few thousandths of a second, far too fast to see. A slow-motion video shows the squash. A ball that does not spring back, like a ball of wet clay, does not bounce at all.
examples: A rubber ball dropped on the floor squashes, springs back and bounces up.
A ball of wet atta dough dropped on the floor goes flat and stays there.
A tennis ball rule says that dropped from 254 cm onto concrete, a good ball must bounce back to between 135 and 147 cm.
explanations.art: A ball shown in three pictures: falling, squashed flat on a floor, and round again, rising.
explanations.context: This card is about bouncing. It says what happens in the moment a ball hits the floor.

explanations.definition: A hard surface lets the ball do the squashing and springing back, so the ball bounces high. A soft surface squashes instead of the ball. It springs back too slowly to push the ball, so the ball bounces low.
explanations.description: In the bounce test, the floor hardly gave way at all. So the ball squashed, sprang back and bounced high. A pillow is soft. When the ball hits it, the pillow squashes instead of the ball. The pillow's cotton or foam rubs on itself as it squashes. That rubbing turns the ball's movement into a little warmth and sound. By the time the pillow comes back up, the ball has stopped. So soft surfaces take the bounce away. This is why a cricket ball bounces higher on a hard, dry pitch than on a soft, damp one.
examples: A ball bounces high off a tiled floor, lower off a doormat, and hardly at all off a pillow.
A cricket ball bounces higher on a hard, dry pitch than on a soft, damp one.
A tennis ball bounces more slowly and higher on a clay court than on a grass court, so players need to play differently.
explanations.art: Two side views: a ball squashed flat on a hard floor, and a ball sitting in a deep dent in a soft pillow.
explanations.context: This card explains the result of the bounce test. It says why a soft surface gives a low bounce.

explanations.definition: No bounce gives back all the energy of the fall. Some of it always turns into warmth and sound, so each bounce is lower than the one before.
explanations.description: Energy is never used up. It only changes from one kind to another. A falling ball has energy of movement. When it bounces, some of that energy turns into warmth in the ball and the floor, and some into the sound of the bounce. Only what is left lifts the ball back up. So a ball bounces lower and lower, and then rolls and stops. Squash players hit their ball against a wall many times before a game. This warms the ball up, and a warm squash ball bounces higher.
examples: A ball left to bounce on its own gets lower each time and then stops.
A squash ball feels warm after a few minutes of play.
You hear a thud with every bounce. That sound is some of the ball's energy, travelling away through the air.
explanations.art: A ball bouncing five times, each bounce lower, with small sound marks at each landing.
explanations.context: This card is about energy. It says why a ball never bounces back as high as it fell from.

explanations.definition: When you run, your foot pushes back and down on the ground, and the ground pushes you forward and up. Your legs also squash and spring back with every step, like a ball.
explanations.description: Each time your foot lands, your knee bends a little and the tendons in your leg stretch. Then they spring back and help lift you into the next step. On a hard road, the ground does not give way, so your legs do the springing. On soft sand, your foot sinks in. The sand moves and does not spring back, so some of your push is lost in it. Your muscles must do more work for every step. Scientists in Belgium measured people walking and running on sand in 1998. Both took more energy than on a hard surface. Grip matters too. Friction between your foot and the ground stops your foot sliding back as you push.
examples: Running on Marina Beach in Chennai is much more tiring than running on the road beside it.
A kangaroo stretches the long tendons in their legs with every hop. The tendons spring back and help lift the kangaroo again, so they can travel far without tiring.
On a smooth wet floor your foot slides back when you try to run, because there is little friction.
explanations.art: A girl running from a hard road onto soft sand, with deep footprints in the sand and shallow ones on the road.
explanations.context: This card is about running. It says what your legs and the ground do with every step.

explanations.concept: Why a thrown ball flies in a curve
explanations.definition: A thrown ball keeps moving forward because of the throw, while gravity pulls it down all the time. Together, these make a curved path called a parabola.
explanations.description: After the ball leaves your hand, nothing pushes it forward any more. It keeps going forward on its own, slowed a little by the air. At the same time, gravity pulls it down, from the very first moment. So the ball's path bends down more and more, in a smooth curve. A faster throw goes further forward before it reaches the ground. The angle matters too. Thrown flat, the ball soon hits the ground. Thrown straight up, it comes back to you. Without air, a throw halfway between flat and straight up, at 45 degrees, goes furthest. In real sport, with air and the thrower's height, the best angle is usually a little lower.
examples: A faster marble rolled off a table lands further from the table.
Water squirting from a hose or a squeezed bottle makes the same curve you can see.
A fielder throwing from the boundary throws the ball up a little, not flat, to reach the wicket keeper.
explanations.art: A dotted curve from a girl's hand, with small arrows along it: one pointing forward and one pointing down at each point.
explanations.context: This card is about throwing. It explains the curved path of a ball through the air.

explanations.concept: Kicking: where you hit the ball
explanations.definition: A kick through the middle of a ball sends it straight without spin. A kick off the middle makes it spin as well as move.
explanations.description: A kick is a short, hard push. If your foot pushes straight through the centre of the ball, the ball goes straight and does not spin. If your foot hits the ball to one side of the centre, part of the push turns the ball, so it spins. A kick under the ball makes it lift into the air, and it often spins backwards too. A harder kick, or a heavier foot moving fast, gives the ball more speed. Footballers use the side of the foot to make the ball spin on purpose.
examples: Flick a light ball at its middle and it rolls straight. Flick it at its side and it spins and turns.
A footballer taking a corner kicks the side of the ball so that it spins and bends towards the goal.
A kick under a ball lifts it high into the air.
explanations.art: Three footballs seen from above, each with a foot touching it in a different place: the middle, the side and underneath, with arrows showing where each goes.
explanations.context: This card is about kicking. It says why the place you kick a ball changes how it moves.

explanations.concept: Why a spinning ball curves in the air
explanations.definition: A spinning ball pushes the air around it to one side, and the air pushes the ball the other way. This is called the Magnus effect, after Heinrich Gustav Magnus, who studied it in 1852.
explanations.description: That a spinning ball curves is measured and agreed. Isaac Newton noticed a spinning tennis ball curving in 1672. Scientists explain why in two ways. Both describe the same thing, but teachers argue about which is clearer. A good way to settle it is to watch a spinning ball yourself, and see which way it curves.
examples: A footballer kicks the side of the ball, and it bends round a wall of players.
In cricket, a spin bowler makes the ball turn sideways when it bounces, and drift a little in the air.
A table tennis ball hit with topspin dips down fast onto the table.

perspectives.explanation: The spinning surface drags the air near it round with it. So air leaving the back of the ball is thrown to one side. The ball pushes the air one way, so the air pushes the ball the other way.

On one side, the ball's surface turns the same way the air flows past, and the air moves faster there. On the other side it turns against the air and slows it. Faster-moving air presses less, so the ball is pushed towards the faster side.

explanations.art: A football seen from above, spinning, with streams of air bending round it and the ball's path curving to one side.
explanations.context: This card is about why a spinning ball bends in the air. Scientists agree that it does, and explain it in two ways.

explanations.definition: To jump, you push down and back on the ground, and the ground pushes you up and forward. To catch softly, you let your hands move back with the ball, so it slows down over a longer time.
explanations.description: When you swing your arms forward and up as you jump, your arms gain forward speed. Your body carries that speed with it into the air. The swing also keeps your legs pushing on the ground for a little longer. So you go further. Catching works the other way round. A ball must be slowed from fast to still. If your hands stay stiff, it stops in a very short time, and the force on your hands is big. If your hands move back with the ball, it takes longer to stop. Then the force is smaller, so the catch stings less and the ball is less likely to bounce out.
examples: A long jumper swings both arms forward as they take off.
A cricketer catching a hard ball pulls their hands back towards their body.
A water balloon caught with stiff hands bursts. Caught with hands that move back, it often stays whole.
explanations.art: Two pictures: a child mid-jump with arms swung forward, and a child catching a ball with hands moving back towards their chest.
explanations.context: This card is about jumping and catching. It says how arms help a jump, and why soft hands make a gentle catch.

agreed.text: A ball bounces when it squashes and springs back. Hard surfaces give a higher bounce than soft ones.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it with one ball and a few surfaces at home. Sports bodies test balls and pitches this way, by dropping balls from a set height and measuring the bounce.

agreed.text: No bounce gives back all the energy of the fall. Some always turns into warmth and sound.
agreed.evidence: No dropped ball ever bounces back to the height it fell from. Careful measurements show the ball and the floor warm up very slightly.

agreed.text: A thrown ball, without air, follows a curve called a parabola.
agreed.evidence: Galileo showed it by experiment and with geometry in 1638. Slow-motion videos and photos taken with flashing lights show the same curve.

agreed.text: Running on soft sand takes more energy than running on a hard surface.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measured the oxygen people breathed while walking and running on sand and on a hard floor. On sand, they used more.

agreed.text: A spinning ball curves in the air.
agreed.evidence: It has been measured in wind tunnels and filmed in slow motion. Newton noticed it in 1672, and Magnus measured it in 1852.

challenging.claim: A heavier ball always bounces higher.
challenging.who: A common guess among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: A heavy cricket ball feels powerful, and a light balloon hardly bounces at all.
challenging.against: How high a ball bounces depends on how elastic it is and on the surface, not on how heavy it is. A light rubber ball bounces far higher than a heavy cricket ball or a steel ball on a tiled floor.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that heavy balls bounce best.

challenging.claim: A thrown ball goes straight until its push runs out, then drops straight down.
challenging.who: Many scholars in Europe before about 1540, and many children today
challenging.for: A hard throw looks almost straight at the start.
challenging.against: Gravity pulls the ball down from the first moment. In the 1500s, Tartaglia argued that the path curves all the way. Galileo showed with experiments that it is a smooth curve, a parabola.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of how a thrown ball moves.

challenging.claim: Training on sand makes you a faster runner on a hard track.
challenging.for: Sand makes leg muscles work harder, and it is gentler on the joints when you land.
challenging.against: Running on sand is slower and feels different, so it may not train the exact movements of a fast run. Studies of sand training are small, and they do not agree.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument among coaches: does running on sand help on the track?

challenging.claim: Running barefoot is better for your feet than running in shoes.
challenging.for: Barefoot runners often land on the front of the foot, which can be gentler. People ran without shoes for most of human history.
challenging.against: Shoes protect feet from glass, thorns and very hot roads. There is not enough evidence that barefoot running prevents injuries.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument: shoes or bare feet for running?

big_questions.q: When a ball lands on a pillow, where does its movement go?
big_questions.hint: Put your hand on the pillow after many drops. Listen to each landing. What did you feel and hear?

big_questions.q: When you push on the ground and the ground pushes you forward, who is doing the running, you or the ground?
big_questions.hint: Try to run on a smooth, slippery floor in socks. What happens when the floor cannot push back?

big_questions.q: Your legs spring like a ball when you run. Which other parts of your body spring back?
big_questions.hint: Jump on the spot and land softly. Which parts bend and straighten?

big_questions.q: A ball thrown on the Moon would fly much further. Why?
big_questions.hint: The Moon pulls things down less than the Earth does, and it has no air.

big_questions.q: Many games, like cricket, kabaddi, lagori and football, are played all over the world in different ways. Why do people everywhere invent games of running, throwing and catching?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a child learns about their own body and the world in each game.

big_questions.q: Every sport is played with forces between the player, the ball and the ground. Is a game something one person does, or something that happens between many things?
big_questions.hint: Try to list everything that pushes on something else in one cricket shot.

story.title: Nila and the Beach Race
story.note: Elliot's Beach is a real beach in Besant Nagar, Chennai, and beach cricket on wet sand is common there. Nila, Arjun, their mother and the race are made up.
text: Sports Day was in two weeks, and Arjun wanted to win the 100 metre race. He was eight, and he had come second last year. 'This year I will train every evening,' he told his sister Nila. 'On the beach, like the big runners in films.'
Nila was ten. She liked to watch things carefully before she believed them. So every evening she walked with Arjun and Amma to Elliot's Beach, carrying her notebook and an old tennis ball.

Arjun ran on the soft, dry sand near the road, from the lifeguard tower to the fishing boats and back. After four runs his face was red and his legs were shaking. 'The sand is too hot,' he said. Next evening it was cooler, and he was just as tired. 'My legs are getting weaker,' he said on the third day, and his lip wobbled.

On Saturday, the school let the children practise on the track. Arjun ran 100 metres while Amma timed him on her phone. He was faster than he had ever been. 'Maybe the beach is working,' Amma said. But Arjun shook his head. 'On the beach I feel slow and heavy,' he said. 'Here I feel like a ball.'
Nila wrote that down. Like a ball. Then she had an idea.

That evening, on the beach, Nila stood on the cement path at the edge of the sand. She held the tennis ball at the height of her nose and let it drop. It bounced back up to her waist. She stepped onto the soft, dry sand and dropped it again from the same height. The ball landed with a soft thump, made a little hollow in the sand and stayed there.

'Arjun, come and see,' she called. She did it three more times on the path and three more times on the sand. On the path, the ball always came back to her waist. On the dry sand, it never came back up at all.
'The sand ate the bounce,' said Arjun.

'It's not eating it,' said Nila. 'Look at the hollow. When the ball lands on the path, the path doesn't move. So the ball squashes and springs back up. When the ball lands on the sand, the sand moves instead. It slides out of the way and doesn't spring back. So nothing pushes the ball up again.'

She walked down to the dark, wet sand near the waves, where some boys were playing cricket. The wet sand was firm and packed down. Nila dropped the ball there. It bounced, not as high as on the path, but much higher than on the dry sand.
'That's why they play cricket down here,' said Amma, who had come to watch. 'On the dry sand the ball would just stop.'

Nila turned to her brother. 'When you run on the track, you said you feel like a ball. When your foot lands, your legs bend a little and then spring back. The track doesn't move, so all of your push goes into the next step. On the dry sand, your foot sinks and the sand slides away. Some of your push goes into the sand, not into you. So every step takes more work.'
Arjun looked at the deep footprints he had left near the tower. Each one had a little heap of sand kicked up behind it.
'So my legs aren't getting weaker?' he asked.
'Your legs are doing more work than on the track,' said Nila. 'The sand makes every step harder. That doesn't mean you are slow.'
Arjun thought about this. 'Then is running on sand good or bad?'
Nila opened her notebook. 'I don't know,' she said. 'It makes your legs work hard. But it's not the same as running on a track. Maybe you should do both.'

So for the next ten days, Arjun ran twice on the dry sand and twice on the firm, wet sand by the waves, where his feet hardly sank. Then on Saturdays he ran on the track. Nila timed him and kept a table in her notebook, with a column for each kind of ground.
On Sports Day, Arjun came first by the length of one long stride. When he got his medal, he ran straight to Nila. 'I didn't feel heavy at all,' he said. 'I felt like your tennis ball on the path.'
Nila smiled and wrote one more line in her notebook: 'The ground runs with you. Hard ground gives your push back. Soft ground keeps some of it.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: a bounce needs something to squash and spring back fast. On the hard path, the ball squashed and sprang back, and the path hardly moved. On dry sand, the sand moved instead: the grains slid apart and did not spring back, so the ball's movement was spent shifting sand and was not returned. Firm wet sand, where water holds the grains together, gave a middling bounce. A runner's legs work like the ball: tendons and muscles stretch and spring back with each step. On soft sand, part of each push goes into moving sand, so running takes more energy. Whether sand training makes a runner faster on a track is still argued about.
ask: Why did the tennis ball bounce on the path but not on the dry sand?
Why do people play beach cricket on the wet sand near the waves?
Arjun said his legs were getting weaker. What was really happening?
How did Nila find out, instead of just guessing?
Nila said 'I don't know' when Arjun asked if sand training was good. Was that a good answer? Why?

games.title: Sports Day Freeze: what is pushing what?
games.context: This is an acting game. Players act out a sport, freeze, and say which forces are acting on their body at that moment.

Tug of war (Hands pull the rope, feet push on the ground)
Running on sand (Feet push, sand slides back, so the push is weaker)

rules: One player picks a card and acts out the sport, without speaking.
When the leader calls 'Freeze!', the actor stops still.
Then the actor says one push or pull acting at that moment. The card's answer helps.
1 point for guessing the sport, 1 point for the actor who names a force correctly.
Play until everyone has acted 3 times.

setup.art: A child frozen mid-run in a living room, one foot pushing back on the floor, while two others point and guess.
setup.caption: 1. Act out a sport. Freeze when the leader calls.

setup.art: The frozen child with arrows drawn on them: the foot pushing back, the floor pushing forward.
setup.caption: 2. Say what is pushing what.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and shuffle them. Clear a space in the room.
flow.say: We will act out sports, then freeze, and say what is pushing what.
flow.kid: Pick a card. Act it out. Freeze when you hear 'Freeze!'

flow.do: Act out 'Running a race' yourself, freeze, and explain the forces.
flow.say: I'm running. Freeze! My foot pushes back on the floor. The floor pushes me forward. That's what moves me.
flow.kid: Watch the grown-up run and freeze. What pushes them forward?

check.q: When you run, which way does your foot push on the ground?
check.why: Your foot pushes back on the ground, and the ground pushes you forward. That's why it is hard to run on a slippery floor or loose sand: the ground can't push back well. Picking 'forward' is a common mix-up, because you move forward.

flow.do: Take turns to act out the cards and freeze. Guess, then name the forces.
flow.say: Freeze! Who can guess the sport? What is pushing what?
flow.kid: Act out your card. Freeze! Say one push or pull.

flow.do: Add up the points.
flow.say: In which sport was the ground most important?
flow.kid: Count the points. Which sport needed the ground most?

experiments.title: The Bounce Test: which floor gives the ball back?
experiments.question: If we drop the same ball from the same height onto different surfaces, which one gives the highest bounce?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put the five surfaces in order, from the one you think gives the highest bounce to the lowest. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same ball every time, and drop it from the same height, 100 cm. Let go without pushing it down. Change only the surface. Drop the ball 3 times on each surface, because one try can be a fluke, and use the middle number.

materials.item: one bouncy ball: a tennis ball, a rubber ball or a plastic cricket ball
a measuring tape or a long ruler, and a strip of paper about 110 cm long, or two sheets of newspaper taped end to end
sticky tape
five surfaces: the bare floor, a doormat or yoga mat, a bedsheet folded into 8 layers, a pillow, and a steel plate with a raised rim filled with dry rice
a phone that can take a slow-motion video, if you have one

experiments.safety: Do this on a dry floor with space around you. Sweep up any rice that spills, so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Make a paper ruler on the wall. Drop one ball 3 times onto each of 5 surfaces. Fill in the table and make a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each surface, as tall as its middle number.
experiments.context: This is the main experiment of the unit. You drop one ball onto five different surfaces and measure how high it bounces from each.

setup.art: A strip of paper taped up a wall from the floor, marked every 10 cm up to 100 cm, with a tiled floor below.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a paper ruler to the wall, marked every 10 cm.

setup.art: A hand holding a tennis ball with its bottom at the 100 cm mark, and a child crouching beside the wall, eyes level with the 50 cm mark.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the ball at 100 cm and let go. A helper watches the top of the bounce.

setup.art: Five surfaces in a row against the wall: bare tiles, a doormat, a folded bedsheet, a pillow and a steel plate of rice.
setup.caption: 3. Do the same on each of the five surfaces.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: a tennis ball dropped from 100 cm

flow.do: 1. Tape the paper strip up a wall, starting at the floor. 2. Use the measuring tape to mark it every 10 cm, up to 100 cm. 3. Write the numbers beside the marks.
flow.say: We need to measure how high the ball bounces. So let's make a tall paper ruler on the wall first.
flow.kid: Tape the paper up the wall from the floor. Mark it every 10 cm. Write the numbers. Stop at 100.
flow.parent: A door or a cupboard side works too, if your walls cannot take tape. Check that the floor below the strip is hard and flat, like tiles, stone or cement.

flow.do: 1. Lay the five surfaces in a row near the wall. 2. Show your child each one, and ask for a guess.
flow.say: Here are five surfaces: the bare floor, a doormat, a folded bedsheet, a pillow and a plate of rice. Which will give the highest bounce? Which the lowest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the five surfaces. Which gives the highest bounce? Which the lowest? Why? Write your order.

ask.q: Why do you think that surface will give the highest bounce?
good: Because the ball bounces well on the floor when I play.

flow.parent: Wait for a guess and a reason. Don't say whether it is right. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ball so its bottom is level with the 100 cm mark. 2. Open your fingers and let it fall, without pushing it down. 3. Your child crouches with their eyes at about the 50 cm mark. 4. They read the mark at the bottom of the ball, at the top of its bounce. 5. Do this 3 times on the bare floor.
flow.say: I will just open my hand. If I push the ball down, it would not be a fair test. You watch the bottom of the ball at the top of its bounce.
flow.kid: Crouch down by the wall. Watch the bottom of the ball. Where does it stop going up? Read the mark.
flow.parent: Reading a bounce by eye is hard. If two of you disagree, take the number in between. A slow-motion phone video, held level with the bounce, makes reading easy. Pause it at the top of the bounce. Write each try in the table.

flow.do: 1. Put the doormat against the wall, under the paper ruler. 2. Drop the ball 3 times and read each bounce. 3. Do the same with the folded bedsheet, the pillow and the plate of rice.
flow.say: Same ball, same height, same way of letting go. Only the surface changes. Let's see what each one does.
flow.kid: Now the doormat. Drop it 3 times. Then the bedsheet, the pillow and the rice. Write each bounce.
flow.parent: Measure from the top of each surface, not from the floor. A folded sheet is about 2 to 3 cm thick, so take that off the reading, or hold the ball 100 cm above the top of the sheet. On the pillow and the rice, the ball may hardly lift at all. That is a real result: write 0 or a small number.

check.q: Lakshmi drops her ball from 100 cm on the floor, but from 50 cm on the pillow. Is that a fair test?
options: Yes, because it is the same ball
No, because the height changed as well as the surface
Yes, because the pillow is soft anyway
check.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. Here both the height and the surface changed. So if the pillow bounce is lower, we can't tell which change caused it. Picking 'same ball' is half right: the ball must be the same, and so must the height.

flow.do: 1. For each surface, find the middle number of the three tries. 2. Draw a bar chart, with one bar for each surface.
flow.say: Let's find the middle number for each surface. If the tries were 50, 55 and 60, the middle one is 55.
flow.kid: Find the middle number for each surface. Draw a bar for each. Which bar is tallest?
flow.parent: The middle number, called the median, is less upset by one odd try than the average is.

flow.do: 1. Drop the ball onto the pillow 10 times quickly. 2. Your child presses the pillow and listens to each landing.
flow.say: The ball fell 100 cm onto the pillow and hardly came back up. Where did its movement go? Listen and feel.
flow.kid: Listen to the ball land on the pillow. Feel the dent. Where did the bounce go?

ask.q: The ball fell fast. On the pillow it stopped and stayed. What happened to the pillow?
good: It went down and came back up slowly.

flow.parent: The warmth is far too small to feel. The dent and the soft thud are what your child will notice. Both are signs of the pillow squashing and rubbing on itself.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: hard surfaces give a high bounce and soft ones give a low bounce. What I saw: on the floor it bounced to about 55 cm, and on the pillow to about 5 cm. Why: on the floor the ball squashed and sprang back up. On the pillow, the pillow squashed instead and did not push the ball back up.

experiments.title: Galileo's Table: does a faster ball land further?
experiments.question: A marble rolls off the edge of a table. If it is moving faster, does it land further from the table?
experiments.predict: Guess first. We will roll a marble from three heights on a ramp, so it leaves the table slowly, faster and fastest. Will it land in the same place each time, or further each time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same marble, the same ramp and the same table each time. Change only how high up the ramp you let go. Let go without pushing. Do each height 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a glass marble
a 30 cm plastic ruler with a groove down the middle, or a strip of stiff card about 40 cm long folded into a V shape
a few thick books, to lift one end of the ramp
a dining table or a study table
a large steel plate or a baking tray, with a thin layer of rava or atta spread on it
a key tied to a piece of thread, to find the spot on the floor right below the table edge
a measuring tape

experiments.safety: Pick up the marble after each try. A marble on the floor can make someone slip, and small children may put it in their mouth.

schedule.what: Roll a marble off the table from three heights on a ramp. Find where it lands in a plate of rava, and measure how far that is from the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the table from the side, with three curved paths, one for each height.
experiments.context: This experiment is about the curved path of a moving ball. Galileo did a test like it about 400 years ago.

setup.art: A grooved ruler on a table, one end lifted on a book, its low end lying flat about 10 cm from the table edge.
setup.caption: 1. Make a ramp that ends a hand's width before the table edge.

setup.art: A key hanging on a thread from the table edge, just touching the floor, and a pencil mark on the floor below it.
setup.caption: 2. Hang a key from the edge to mark the spot right below it.

setup.art: A marble flying off the table edge in a curve and landing in a steel plate of rava on the floor, leaving a small dent.
setup.caption: 3. Roll the marble. It leaves a dent where it lands.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results, with a table 75 cm high

flow.do: 1. Lay the ruler on the table with its low end about 10 cm from the edge. 2. Lift the other end on books. 3. Hang the key on its thread from the table edge, so it just touches the floor. 4. Mark that spot on the floor with a pencil or a bit of tape.
flow.say: The marble will roll down the ramp, run across the flat bit of table, and fly off the edge. We need to know where 'right below the edge' is, so we can measure from there.
flow.kid: Set the ramp up. Hang the key from the edge. Mark the spot under it.
flow.parent: The flat gap of table between the ramp and the edge matters. It makes the marble leave the edge moving flat, not downwards, so the three tries are fair.

flow.do: 1. Mark three start points on the ramp, 5 cm, 10 cm and 20 cm above the table. 2. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: From higher up the ramp, the marble will be going faster when it leaves the table. Will it land in the same place, or further away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Higher up the ramp means faster. Where will it land each time? Why?

ask.q: Where do you think the fastest marble will land?
good: In the same place, because it falls the same height.

flow.parent: Measure the start heights straight up from the table top with the ruler, not along the ramp. Both guesses are common and sensible. Let the test decide.

flow.do: 1. Put the plate of rava on the floor in front of the table. 2. Roll the marble once from 10 cm to see where it lands. 3. Move the plate so that spot is in the middle.
flow.say: This first roll is a practice, to find where to put the plate.
flow.kid: Practice roll first. Move the plate to where the marble lands.
flow.parent: Smooth the rava flat with your hand after each try, so each new dent is easy to see.

flow.do: 1. Let go of the marble from the 5 cm mark, 3 times. 2. Each time, measure from the floor mark to the dent. 3. Do the same from 10 cm and from 20 cm, moving the plate if needed.
flow.say: Just open your fingers, don't push. Watch the path of the marble as it falls. Is it straight down, or a curve?
flow.kid: Let go from 5 cm. Measure to the dent. Then 10 cm. Then 20 cm.

check.q: As the marble flies off the table, what path does it follow?
options: A curve that bends down more and more
Straight down, right below the edge
check.why: The marble keeps moving forward, and gravity pulls it down from the very first moment. So its path curves down more and more. 'Straight out, then straight down' was what many people believed before Galileo's time. If you saw that, watch again closely: the bend starts right at the edge.

flow.parent: The marble flies fast. Your child may only see a blur. A slow-motion phone video, taken from the side, shows the curve clearly.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the table from the side, with three curved paths ending at the three dents.
flow.say: Draw the three paths. Do they all start in the same place? Where do they end?
flow.kid: Draw the table from the side. Draw three paths. Where does each end?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a faster ball goes further before it lands. What I saw: from 5 cm the marble landed about 30 cm from the table, and from 20 cm about 58 cm. Why: the marble keeps moving forward while gravity pulls it down. The faster one went further forward in the same short time it took to fall.

experiments.title: Arms or No Arms: does swinging your arms help you jump further?
experiments.question: Do you jump further from standing if you swing your arms, or if you keep them still behind your back?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will swinging your arms make your jump longer, shorter, or the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same child jumps from the same line, on the same floor, both ways. Change only what the arms do. Jump 3 times each way, and rest a little between jumps, so tiredness does not spoil the test.

materials.item: a clear stretch of dry floor at least 2 metres long, such as a corridor
sticky tape, to make a start line
a measuring tape
a coin or a small eraser, to mark where the back heel lands

experiments.safety: Jump barefoot on a dry floor, never in socks on tiles. Move rugs, toys and furniture away from the landing place. A grown-up watches every jump.

schedule.what: Do 3 standing long jumps with arms held behind your back, and 3 with arms swinging. Measure each one.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw yourself jumping both ways.
experiments.context: This experiment is about jumping. You find out whether your arms help your legs.

setup.art: A strip of tape across a corridor floor, with a child's bare toes just behind it.
setup.caption: 1. Stand with your toes behind the tape line.

setup.art: A child mid-jump with hands clasped behind their back, and the same child mid-jump with both arms swung forward and up.
setup.caption: 2. Jump 3 times with arms behind you, then 3 times swinging them.

setup.art: A coin on the floor at the back of a child's heel after a landing, and a measuring tape from the start line to the coin.
setup.caption: 3. Mark your back heel. Measure from the line.

flow.do: 1. Stick a tape line across the floor. 2. Clear 2 metres of floor in front of it. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: You will jump from this line with both feet together. First with your hands held behind your back. Then swinging your arms. Will your arms make any difference? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Arms behind you, or arms swinging. Which jump will be longer? Why?
flow.parent: Check the floor is dry and your child is barefoot. Socks on tiles are slippery.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds their hands together behind their back. 2. They bend their knees and jump forward with both feet. 3. Put the coin at the back of the heel nearest the line. 4. Measure from the line to the coin. 5. Do 3 jumps, resting a little between them.
flow.say: Hands behind your back. Bend your knees. Jump! Stay where you land, so I can mark your heel.
flow.kid: Hands behind your back. Bend your knees. Jump with both feet. Stay still!
flow.parent: Measure to the heel that lands closest to the line. If your child falls back onto their hands, measure to the hand, as long jump judges do, or do the jump again.

flow.do: 1. Now your child swings both arms back, then forward and up as they jump. 2. Mark and measure in the same way. 3. Do 3 jumps.
flow.say: This time, swing both arms back as you bend, and throw them forward and up as you jump.
flow.kid: Swing your arms back. Bend. Throw your arms forward and up as you jump!

check.q: Meenakshi jumped 3 times with arms swinging and got 110, 115 and 112 cm. What is her middle number?
check.why: Put the three in order: 110, 112, 115. The middle one is 112 cm. Picking 115 means choosing the best jump, which hides how she usually jumps.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: swinging my arms helps me jump further. What I saw: with my arms behind my back I jumped about 95 cm, and with them swinging about 112 cm. Why: my arms swung forward fast, and my body carried that speed with it into the air. Most children jump further with their arms, often by 10 to 20 cm. If your child did not, they may not yet time the swing with the jump. That is a good thing to practise.

activities.title: Jog on the Spot: hard floor or soft mattress?

materials.item: a mattress or a thick folded quilt laid flat on the floor, not on a bed

activities.safety: Put the mattress on the floor, away from furniture corners. Never jump on a bed. A grown-up stays close.

schedule.what: Jog on the spot 30 steps on the hard floor, then 30 steps on a mattress. Notice which is harder work.

activities.record: Write which was harder, and one thing your legs or feet felt.
activities.context: This is a quick activity to start the unit. You feel for yourself how the ground changes running.

setup.art: A child jogging on the spot on a tiled floor, knees lifting.
setup.caption: 1. Jog on the spot 30 steps on the hard floor.

setup.art: The same child jogging on a mattress laid on the floor, feet sinking in.
setup.caption: 2. Now jog 30 steps on a mattress on the floor.

flow.do: Your child jogs on the spot on the bare floor, lifting their knees, for 30 steps. Count with them.
flow.say: Jog on the spot, knees up. Let's count 30 steps together. Notice how your feet and legs feel.
flow.kid: Jog on the spot. Lift your knees. Count 30 steps. How do your legs feel?

flow.do: Your child jogs 30 steps on the mattress, at the same speed. Count with them.
flow.say: Now the same on the mattress, at the same speed. Is it easier or harder?
flow.kid: Now jog on the mattress. Same speed. Easier or harder?
flow.parent: Most children find the mattress harder and wobblier. Their feet sink in, and they have to lift them out each time.

flow.do: Ask both questions and wait for answers. Don't explain yet.
flow.say: Which was harder? What did your feet do on the mattress that they didn't do on the floor? Why do you think it was harder?
flow.kid: Which was harder? What did your feet do on the mattress? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the mattress was harder?
good: It didn't push me back up.

flow.parent: Keep the answer as a question for later. The bounce test will help your child explain it.

activities.title: Watch the Curve: a toss and a water jet

materials.item: a soft ball, or a pair of socks rolled into a ball
an empty plastic bottle with its cap
a pin or a thin nail, to make a hole in the bottle
a bucket, in the bathroom or on the balcony

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in the bottle. Do the water part in the bathroom or on the balcony.

schedule.what: Toss a soft ball to each other and watch its path. Then squeeze a bottle with a hole and watch the water's path.

activities.record: Draw the path of the ball and the path of the water. Are they the same shape?
activities.context: This activity is about the path of a thrown thing. A water jet shows the whole curve at once.

setup.art: A mother and a girl tossing a rolled pair of socks to each other across a room, with a dotted curve between them.
setup.caption: 1. Toss a soft ball gently to each other. Watch its path.

setup.art: A plastic bottle with a small hole near the bottom, squeezed over a bucket, with a curved jet of water arcing into the bucket.
setup.caption: 2. Squeeze a bottle with a hole. Watch the water's path.

flow.do: 1. Stand about 3 metres apart. 2. Toss the soft ball gently to each other 5 times. 3. Your child watches the ball's path, not the catcher.
flow.say: Watch the ball, not me. Does it go in a straight line, or does it bend?
flow.kid: Throw the ball gently. Watch it fly. Straight line, or bending?

flow.do: 1. Make a small hole in the side of the bottle, near the bottom. 2. Fill it with water and put the cap on. 3. Hold it over the bucket and squeeze gently, then harder.
flow.say: Water comes out in tiny drops, one after another. Each drop is like a tiny thrown ball. So the jet shows us the whole path at once. What happens when I squeeze harder?
flow.kid: Squeeze the bottle over the bucket. See the water's path? Now squeeze harder.

ask.q: When you squeeze harder, what happens to the water's path?
good: It is faster, so it lands further away.

flow.parent: Hold the bottle level, so the jet starts out flat. A harder squeeze makes the water leave faster, so the jet reaches further before it falls into the bucket.

flow.do: Your child draws both paths side by side.
flow.say: Draw the ball's path and the water's path. Are they the same shape?
flow.kid: Draw the ball's path. Draw the water's path. Same shape?

check.q: Why does the water jet bend down?
options: Gravity pulls each drop down as it moves forward
check.why: Each drop keeps moving forward from the squeeze, while gravity pulls it down all the time. That makes the curve. Water does not get tired, and a bucket has no pull of its own on the water.

activities.title: Kick It Off the Middle: make a ball spin

materials.item: a light plastic ball or a table tennis ball
a smooth floor

activities.safety: Use a light ball indoors, away from glass and the TV.

schedule.what: Flick a light ball on the floor at its middle and at its side. Watch how it moves each time.

activities.record: Draw the ball from above with an arrow for each flick: middle and side.
activities.context: This activity is about kicking. You flick a ball with your finger, like a tiny kick, and see what happens when you hit it off the middle.

setup.art: A finger flicking a table tennis ball right at its middle on a smooth floor, with a straight arrow ahead of it.
setup.caption: 1. Flick the ball right at its middle.

setup.art: A finger flicking the same ball on its side, with a curved arrow showing it spinning and turning away.
setup.caption: 2. Flick it at its side. Does it spin?

flow.do: Your child puts the ball on the floor and flicks it with a finger, right at its middle, 3 times.
flow.say: A flick is like a tiny kick. Flick it right at its middle. Where does it go?
flow.kid: Flick the ball right at its middle. Where does it go?

flow.do: Now your child flicks the ball at its side, 3 times. Then flicks it low down, near the floor, 3 times.
flow.say: Now flick it at the side. Then low down. Does it go straight? Does it spin?
flow.kid: Flick it at the side. Then low down. Does it spin?

ask.q: What changed when you flicked it off the middle?

flow.parent: A flick at the side makes the ball spin and move off at an angle. A flick low down can make it hop. Draw a dot on the ball with a pen to see the spin easily.

flow.do: Ask how a footballer could make a ball spin on purpose.
flow.say: Footballers kick the side of the ball on purpose. Why do you think they want it to spin?
flow.kid: Why would a footballer want the ball to spin?

check.q: Farhan kicks a football right through its middle. What will the ball most likely do?
check.why: A push through the centre moves the ball without turning it. A push to one side of the centre turns it as well, so it spins. If you picked 'spin fast', try the flick again right at the middle, and watch the dot.

activities.title: Soft Hands: catch a water balloon

materials.item: 3 or 4 small balloons filled with water

activities.safety: Do this in the bathroom, on a balcony, or outside. Pick up every bit of burst balloon, because small children can choke on balloon pieces.

schedule.what: Catch a gently tossed water balloon, first with stiff hands, then with hands that move back with it.

activities.record: Write what happened with stiff hands and with soft hands.
activities.context: This activity is about catching. You find out why good catchers pull their hands back.

setup.art: A small water balloon in the air, gently tossed between two people on a balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Toss a water balloon gently.

setup.art: A child's hands moving back towards their chest as they catch a water balloon, with an arrow showing the hands moving back.
setup.caption: 2. Catch it with hands that move back with it.

flow.do: Fill the balloons about half full with water and tie them. Stand about 2 metres apart.
flow.say: We will catch water balloons. First with stiff hands that don't move, then with soft hands that move back with the balloon. Which way will burst more? Why?
flow.kid: Stiff hands or soft hands. Which will burst the balloon? Why?

flow.do: Toss a balloon gently. Your child catches it with stiff hands that stay still.
flow.say: Hold your hands out and keep them still, like a wall.
flow.kid: Keep your hands still, like a wall. Catch!

flow.do: Toss another balloon the same way. Your child lets their hands move back towards their chest as they catch.
flow.say: This time, let your hands go back with the balloon as it lands in them.
flow.kid: Now let your hands move back as you catch. Soft hands!
flow.parent: Stiff hands stop the balloon in a very short time, so the push on it is big, and it often bursts. Moving hands back makes the stop take longer, so the push is smaller.

flow.do: Ask what was different.
flow.say: What was different between the two catches? Where else do people use soft hands?
flow.kid: What was different? Where else do people catch with soft hands?

check.q: Why does a cricketer pull their hands back when they catch a hard ball?
options: So the ball slows down over a longer time and hurts less
check.why: Pulling the hands back makes the ball take longer to stop. Then the force on the hands is smaller, so it stings less and the ball is less likely to bounce out. Stiff hands stop it quickly, with a big force.

activities.title: Sport Spotting: watch a match like a scientist

materials.item: a cricket, football, kabaddi or tennis match on TV or a phone, or a game in a nearby playground
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: If you watch a game outside, stay at the edge, away from the ball.

schedule.what: Watch 10 minutes of a match. Spot bounces, curved throws, spinning balls, soft catches and players pushing on the ground.

activities.record: Make a tally: one mark for each thing you spot.
activities.context: This activity takes everything in the unit to a real game. You look for the physics while you watch.

setup.art: A child on a sofa watching a cricket match on TV, with a notebook of tally marks on their knee.
setup.caption: 1. Watch a match for 10 minutes.

setup.art: A page with five rows: bounce, curved throw, spin, soft catch, push on the ground, each with tally marks.
setup.caption: 2. Make a tally of what you spot.

flow.do: Draw five rows in the notebook: bounce, curved throw, spin, soft catch, push on the ground.
flow.say: Let's watch a match like scientists. Each time you spot one of these, make a mark.
flow.kid: Draw five rows. Bounce, curved throw, spin, soft catch, push on the ground.

flow.do: Watch the match together for 10 minutes. Pause it when your child spots something, and ask them to say what is pushing on what.
flow.say: What did you spot? What pushed on what? Why did it move that way?
flow.kid: Make a mark each time you spot one. Say what pushed what.
flow.parent: In cricket, watch the ball bounce off the pitch, the fielders throw in curves, and the bowler's run-up. In football, look for curving kicks. In kabaddi, see how raiders push off the mat to turn fast.

flow.do: Count the tallies together.
flow.say: Which did you spot most? Which surprised you?
flow.kid: Count your marks. Which did you see most?

projects.title: Build a Rubber Band Ball, and test it on every floor

materials.item: about 150 rubber bands
a crumpled sheet of newspaper, for the middle
the paper ruler on the wall from the bounce test

projects.safety: Rubber bands can snap and sting. Keep them away from faces and eyes. Keep loose bands away from small children.

schedule.what: Crumple a small ball of newspaper. Wrap rubber bands round it, one by one, until it is the size of a tennis ball. Test its bounce on the floor at 50 bands and at 100 bands.
Finish the ball. Test it on the five surfaces from the bounce test, and compare it with your first ball.

projects.record: Write the bounce on the floor after every 50 bands. On day 2, add a row to your bounce table for the new ball.
projects.context: In this 2-day project you make your own ball and find out how it bounces.

setup.art: Hands wrapping rubber bands around a small crumpled ball of newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap rubber bands round a ball of newspaper.

setup.art: A rubber band ball the size of a tennis ball, bouncing beside the paper ruler on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Test the bounce as the ball grows.

flow.do: Crumple half a sheet of newspaper into a tight ball, about the size of a lemon. Drop it from 100 cm and measure the bounce.
flow.say: A newspaper ball hardly bounces. Will it bounce better with rubber bands round it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Drop the paper ball. Does it bounce? Will rubber bands help? Why?

flow.do: Wrap rubber bands round the ball, one at a time, crossing them in different directions. Test the bounce after 50 bands and after 100.
flow.say: Cross each band a different way, so the ball stays round. After 50 bands, let's test it.
flow.kid: Wrap the bands round. Cross them different ways. Test after 50.
flow.parent: Double the bands over when they are loose. The ball usually bounces better once the paper is hidden under a thick rubber layer.

flow.do: Write the bounces in a table.
flow.say: Did more bands make a bigger bounce? Why?
flow.kid: Write each bounce. Did more bands help?

check.q: Why does a rubber band ball bounce better than a newspaper ball?
options: Rubber is elastic, so it springs back after it squashes
check.why: Rubber springs back fast after it squashes, so it pushes on the floor and the ball goes back up. Crumpled paper squashes and stays squashed. Weight is not what makes a bounce.

flow.do: On day 2, finish the ball. Drop it on the five surfaces from the bounce test, 3 times each.
flow.say: Does your ball do the same as the first ball on the pillow and the rice?
flow.kid: Test your ball on all five surfaces. Same pattern as before?

challenges.title: The Bounciest Floor: make a mini trampoline
challenges.problem: A pillow takes the bounce away, but a trampoline is soft and gives the bounce back. Make a small surface, softer than the floor, that still gives a ball a good bounce.
constraints: Drop the ball from 100 cm, as in the bounce test.
Your surface must squash when the ball lands. You should see it move.
materials: a steel vessel or a bucket
an old cloth, a balloon cut open, or a plastic bag
the paper ruler from the bounce test
general: Stretch a cloth tight over the mouth of a bucket and tie it with string, like a drum.
Stretch a cut balloon over a steel tumbler or small vessel with a rubber band.
Pull a plastic bag tight between two chairs and tape it.
creative: A trampoline uses springs round the edge. Try hooking rubber bands between the cloth and the bucket handle.
Try the same cloth stretched tight, then a little loose. Which gives the higher bounce?
A drum skin springs back fast. Does a bigger drum give a better bounce than a small one?
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own mini trampoline. Draw it, build it and drop the ball on it. Does it beat the pillow? Does it beat the floor?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You make a soft surface that springs back quickly, like a trampoline.

setup.art: A cloth stretched tight over the mouth of a bucket and tied with string.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch a cloth tight over a bucket.

setup.art: A ball being dropped onto the stretched cloth beside the paper ruler on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Drop the ball from 100 cm and measure the bounce.

flow.do: Remind your child of the bounce test. Read the problem together.
flow.say: The pillow squashed and gave no bounce back. A trampoline is soft too, but it springs back fast. Can you make one?
flow.kid: A pillow takes the bounce away. A trampoline gives it back. Can you make one?

flow.do: Your child builds one of the ideas, or their own, and tests it.
flow.say: Build it, then drop the ball from 100 cm. What bounce do you get?
flow.kid: Build it. Drop the ball from 100 cm. Measure the bounce.
flow.parent: A tightly stretched cloth springs back fast and often gives a good bounce. A loose one sags and acts more like the pillow.

flow.do: Try one change, such as tighter or looser, and test again.
flow.say: What one change will make it better? Try it. Why did that help?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Better or worse? Why?

check.q: Why does a tight trampoline give a better bounce than a pillow?
options: It springs back fast enough to push the ball up
It is harder than the floor
check.why: Both squash when the ball lands. The tight cloth springs back fast, while the ball is still touching it, so it pushes the ball up. The pillow springs back too slowly. A trampoline is softer than the floor, not harder.

challenges.title: Feet for Sand: how not to sink
challenges.problem: Soft sand is hard to walk and run on, because feet sink in. Camels walk across deserts of soft sand every day. Find a way for a 'foot' to sink less into soft ground.
constraints: Use a tray of dry rava, atta or sand as the soft ground.
Use the same weight on each foot you test, such as a full water bottle.
Measure how deep each foot sinks.
materials: a tray or plate of dry rava, atta or sand, at least 3 cm deep
a full 500 ml water bottle, as the weight
cardboard, bottle caps, a steel katori, plastic lids
general: Stand the bottle straight on the rava and see how deep it sinks.
Tape a wide piece of cardboard under the bottle, and test again.
Try a plastic lid, a katori and a bottle cap as feet.
creative: Camels need to cross soft sand to reach food and water. Their feet are wide, with a thick pad that spreads out as they step. Copy that with a soft, wide foot.
People in snowy places wear wide snowshoes to walk on snow. Design a sand-shoe.
Does a foot with holes in it sink more or less than a solid one?
challenges.your_turn: Now design a foot that sinks least. Draw it, make it and test it with the same bottle. What made it work?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You find out how to stop a foot sinking into soft ground, as a camel's feet do.

setup.art: A full water bottle standing on a tray of rava, sunk a little way in.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a full bottle on the rava. See how deep it sinks.

setup.art: The same bottle taped onto a wide square of cardboard, resting on top of the rava without sinking.
setup.caption: 2. Give it a wide foot. Does it sink less?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Stand the bottle on the rava and measure the dent.
flow.say: A camel walks on soft sand every day without sinking much. Let's see how deep the bottle sinks first.
flow.kid: Stand the bottle on the rava. How deep does it sink?
flow.parent: Smooth the rava flat before each test. Lower the bottle gently each time, so each test is fair.

flow.do: Your child tries different feet under the bottle and measures each dent.
flow.say: Try a wide foot, a small foot, a soft foot. Which sinks least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Try different feet. Measure each dent. Which sinks least?

flow.do: Talk about the camel.
flow.say: A camel's feet are wide and padded. How does that help them cross the desert?
flow.kid: How do wide feet help a camel?

check.q: Why does a wide foot sink less into soft sand?
options: The same weight is spread over more sand
check.why: The bottle weighs the same with any foot. A wide foot spreads that weight over more sand, so each bit of sand is pressed less. So it sinks less. The foot does not make the bottle lighter.
