quiz.p: Divya drops a ball from the same height onto a tiled floor and onto a folded quilt. What will she see?
opts: A higher bounce on the tiles
A higher bounce on the quilt
quiz.why: On the tiles the ball squashes and springs back. On the quilt, the quilt squashes instead and gives the bounce back too slowly. Picking 'quilt' often means thinking soft things are bouncy, but softness takes a bounce away unless the surface springs back fast.

quiz.p: Why does a ball of wet clay not bounce, even on a hard floor?
quiz.why: A bounce needs the ball to spring back. Wet clay is not elastic, so it stays flat. Weight is not the problem: a heavier rubber ball still bounces.

quiz.p: In a bounce test, Kavya changes the surface and the height of the drop at the same time. What is wrong?
opts: She can't tell which change made the difference
She should use a smaller ball
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If two things change, you can't tell which one made the bounce different.

quiz.p: Lakshmi's three bounces on the mat were 30 cm, 36 cm and 33 cm. What is the middle number?
quiz.why: In order they are 30, 33 and 36, so the middle number is 33 cm. Picking 36 means choosing the highest, not the middle.

quiz.p: Arjun, a boy of 8, runs on soft beach sand. Why does it tire him faster than running on the road?
opts: Some of each push goes into moving the sand
quiz.why: Soft sand slides away and doesn't spring back, so part of each push is lost in it. His muscles must do more work for each step. Sand doesn't pull feet down, it just gives way under them.

quiz.p: When you run, what in your legs stretches and springs back like a rubber band?
quiz.why: Tendons, like the Achilles tendon at the back of your heel, stretch when your foot lands and spring back as you push off.

quiz.p: Why does a thrown ball fly in a curve?
opts: It keeps moving forward while gravity pulls it down
The air lifts it up and then drops it
It goes straight until its push runs out, then drops
quiz.why: The ball keeps going forward from the throw, while gravity pulls it down from the very start. Together these make a curve. 'Straight until its push runs out' is the old idea that Tartaglia and Galileo showed was wrong.

quiz.p: Meenakshi rolls a marble off a table, first slowly and then fast. Where does the fast one land?
quiz.why: Both take the same short time to fall to the floor. The fast one goes further forward in that time.

quiz.p: Farhan wants to make a football curve round a wall of players. Where should he kick it?
opts: On its side, so it spins
quiz.why: A kick off the middle makes the ball spin. A spinning ball pushes air to one side, and the air pushes the ball the other way, so it curves. A kick through the middle sends it straight.

quiz.p: What is the name for the way a spinning ball curves in the air?
quiz.why: It is named after Heinrich Gustav Magnus, who studied it in 1852. Gravity pulls the ball down, but it doesn't make it curve sideways.

quiz.p: Why do you jump further when you swing your arms forward?
opts: Your arms add forward speed and help your legs push longer
Swinging your arms makes the floor bouncier
quiz.why: Your swinging arms gain forward speed, and your body carries it into the air. The swing also keeps your legs pushing on the floor a little longer. Your weight does not change.

quiz.p: Why does a cricketer pull their hands back when catching?
opts: The ball slows down over a longer time, so the force is smaller
quiz.why: Moving the hands back makes the stop take longer, so the push on the hands is smaller. The catch stings less and the ball is less likely to bounce out.

quiz.p: Tartaglia was an Italian mathematician who taught himself. What did he say about the path of a cannonball?
opts: No part of it is really straight, because its weight pulls it down all the time
It goes in a straight line for ever
It goes straight, then drops straight down
quiz.why: Many people before him thought the path was straight and then dropped like a hook. Tartaglia argued it curves all the way, and Galileo later showed with experiments that it is a smooth curve called a parabola.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3 in Madurai, drops the same tennis ball from the same height onto a stone floor and onto a sofa cushion. Where will it bounce higher?
items.why: On the hard floor the ball squashes and springs back, so it bounces high. The cushion squashes instead and springs back too slowly to push the ball up. A strong answer says what squashes in each case.

items.p: Divya says, 'A ball bounces only because the floor is hard.' Is she right?
items.why: False. The ball must be elastic too. A ball of wet clay on a hard floor does not bounce at all. A bounce needs a ball that springs back and a surface that does not take the squash instead.

items.p: A material that springs back to its old shape after it is squashed is called ____.
items.why: Elastic means it springs back. Rubber is elastic. Dough and wet clay are not.

items.p: Priya drops a rubber ball onto each of these. Sort them: a high bounce or a low bounce?
items: a tiled floor
High bounce
a pillow
Low bounce
a cement road
High bounce
a plate of dry rice
Low bounce
a steel plate on the floor
High bounce
a folded quilt
Low bounce
items.a: see items
items.why: Hard surfaces that hardly give way let the ball spring back. Soft surfaces squash instead of the ball and take the bounce away. A strong answer sorts by how soft the surface is.

items.p: In the bounce test, the ball hardly bounced on the pillow. Explain why. Use the words 'squash' and 'spring back'.
items.a: When the ball landed on the pillow, the pillow squashed instead of the ball. The pillow springs back too slowly to push the ball up again, so the ball hardly bounced.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pillow, not the ball, did the squashing, and that it did not spring back fast enough.

items.p: Put the steps of the bounce test in order.
items: Hold the ball at the 100 cm mark
Tape a paper ruler to the wall
Read how high the ball bounced
Let go without pushing
a: Tape a paper ruler to the wall
Hold the ball at the 100 cm mark
Read how high the ball bounced
items.why: First make the ruler, then hold the ball at the same height each time, let it fall freely, and read the top of the bounce.

items.p: Arjun, a boy of 8, runs on soft beach sand and then on a hard road. Why is the sand more tiring?
opts: His feet sink in, and the sand slides away instead of pushing back
Sand is heavier than the road
items.why: On sand, part of each push goes into moving the sand, so his legs must do more work for every step. On the road, the ground does not give way, and his legs spring back. Roads do not pull anyone along.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: moving back off a surface after hitting it
the pull of the Earth on everything
the grip between two things that touch
turning round and round while moving
a test where you change only one thing
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each from a game.

items.p: Draw the path of a ball thrown gently from your hand to a friend's hands across the room.
items.a: A smooth curve that rises from the thrower's hand, bends over and comes down to the catcher's hands.
items.why: The ball keeps moving forward while gravity pulls it down, so its path is a curve, not a straight line or a hook.
items.art: Two stick figures standing apart, with empty space between them.

items.p: Meenakshi squeezes a plastic bottle with a hole in it, and water squirts out. She squeezes harder. What happens to the jet?
items.why: A harder squeeze makes the water leave faster. Faster water goes further forward before gravity brings it down.

items.p: A thrown ball keeps moving forward after it leaves your hand, even though nothing is pushing it forward.
items.why: True. A moving thing keeps moving until a force slows it. The air slows it a little, and gravity pulls it down, but nothing has to keep pushing it forward.

items.p: Three of these make a gentle catch. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Holding your hands stiff and still
Pulling your hands back as the ball lands
Catching close to your body and letting your arms bend
Bending your knees as you catch
items.why: Stiff hands stop the ball in a very short time, so the force is big and it stings. The other three all let the ball slow down over a longer time.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi argue about which floor is best for a game of catch-the-bounce.

views.says: The tiled floor is best. The ball bounces high, so the game is fast.
The mat is best. The ball bounces lower, so it is easier to catch, and nobody slips.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you found in the bounce test. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the bounce test: the ball bounced higher on the hard floor than on the mat. It picks a side for a reason, such as a fast game or an easy catch. It also gives the other friend her due: both are right about what each floor does.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer uses evidence from the test and sees that the best floor depends on what you want from the game.

items.p: The Earth's pull that brings every thrown ball back down is called ____.
items.why: Gravity pulls everything towards the ground. That is why a thrown ball always comes down.

items.p: Lakshmi drops her ball 3 times on the doormat. It bounces to 38 cm, 42 cm and 40 cm. What is the middle number, and why do we drop it 3 times?
items.a: In order, the numbers are 38, 40 and 42, so the middle number is 40 cm. We drop it 3 times because one try can be a fluke, for example if the ball lands on a bump.
items.why: A strong answer puts the numbers in order to find the middle one, and gives a reason for repeating a test.

items.p: Label the picture of a running leg: the foot pushes ____ on the ground, and the ground pushes the runner ____.
items.why: Your foot pushes back on the ground, and the ground pushes you forward. That is why you can't run well on a slippery floor.
items.art: A side view of a runner's leg with a foot on the ground and two blank arrow labels.

items.p: Fatima, a girl in Hyderabad, drops a ball onto a pillow 20 times in a row. Where does most of the ball's movement go?
opts: Into a little warmth and sound in the pillow
It is destroyed and gone for ever
items.why: Energy is never used up. It changes kind. As the pillow squashes, its cotton or foam rubs on itself, and that turns the movement into a little warmth and sound. Picking 'destroyed' is a common idea, but energy never just vanishes.

items.p: Why is the beach cricket played on the wet sand near the waves, and not on the soft, dry sand? Use the word 'bounce'.
items.a: Wet sand is packed hard, so it does not move much when the ball lands. The ball can squash and spring back, so it bounces. Dry sand slides away under the ball, so it hardly bounces at all.
items.why: A strong answer links the firmness of the ground to the bounce.

items.p: A coach and a runner in Mysuru argue about training on sand.

views.says: Sand makes your legs work harder. Train on sand, and you will be stronger on the track.
Running on sand feels slow and different. I want to train the way I will race, on a hard track.
Running on sand does take more energy. But studies of whether it makes you faster on a track are small, and they don't agree.

items.ask: Whose side are you on? Give a reason. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as 'sand makes my legs work harder' or 'I should practise the movement I will race with'. It also gives another side its due, for example that the scientist is honest that nobody knows for sure. Doing some of both, as Arjun did in the story, is a fair answer too.
items.why: This is a real argument among coaches. A strong answer uses the physics: sand gives back less of each push, so it is harder work, but harder work is not the same as practising a fast run.

items.p: A heavy steel ball always bounces higher than a light rubber ball on a tiled floor.
items.why: False. How high a ball bounces depends on how elastic it is and on the surface, not on its weight. A light rubber ball springs back fast and bounces much higher. A heavy steel ball on tiles may even crack the tile.

items.p: In the Galileo's Table test, Nithya rolls a marble off a table from 5 cm, 10 cm and 20 cm up the ramp. Which marble lands furthest from the table?
opts: They all land in the same place
items.why: From higher up the ramp the marble is moving faster when it leaves the table. All three take the same short time to fall, but the faster one goes further forward in that time.

items.p: Draw a table from the side. Draw the paths of two marbles rolling off it: one slow and one fast. Show where each lands.
items.a: Two curves starting at the table edge. The slow one curves down steeply and lands close to the table. The fast one goes further out before curving down and lands further away.
items.why: Both marbles are pulled down by gravity from the moment they leave the table. The fast one goes further forward while it falls.
items.art: A side view of a table standing on the floor, with empty space in front of it.

items.p: Match each sport to the push that makes it work.
pairs: your foot pushes back on the ground
your feet push down and back, and your arms swing forward
your hands move back to slow the ball gently
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: In every sport, you push on something and it pushes you back, or you slow something over time. A strong answer could explain one of them in a sentence.

items.p: A falling ball hits a hard floor and bounces. Put what happens in order.
items: The ball springs back to round
The ball hits the floor
The ball squashes flat at the bottom
The ball rises into the air
a: The ball squashes flat at the bottom
The ball springs back to round
The ball rises into the air
items.why: The ball squashes as it hits, then springs back, and that springing back pushes it up off the floor. All of this takes a few thousandths of a second.

items.p: Anjali kicks a football on its side, not through its middle. What will the ball do?
opts: Spin as it moves, and may curve in the air
Go perfectly straight with no spin
items.why: A push to one side of the centre turns the ball as well as moving it, so it spins. A spinning ball pushes the air to one side, and the air pushes the ball the other way, so it curves.

items.p: In the arm swing test, most children jump further when they swing their arms. Explain why.
items.a: When you swing your arms forward and up, they gain forward speed. Your body carries that speed into the air. The swing also keeps your legs pushing on the ground a little longer. So you go further.
items.why: A strong answer says the arms add forward movement and help the legs push for longer.

items.p: The curved path of a thrown ball, when there is no air to slow it, is called a ____.
items.why: A parabola is the smooth curve that every thrown thing would follow without air. Galileo proved this in 1638.

items.p: Sort these. Does the ground push back well, or does it give way?
items: a running track
Pushes back well
soft beach sand
Gives way
a cement road
Pushes back well
a thick mattress on the floor
Gives way
firm wet sand near the waves
Pushes back well
deep mud
Gives way
items.a: see items
items.why: Firm ground hardly moves when you push on it, so your push comes back to you. Soft ground moves and does not spring back, so some of your push is lost in it. Wet sand is firmer than dry sand, because the water holds the grains together.

items.p: On a smooth floor in socks, it is hard to start running because there is little friction to stop your foot sliding back.
items.why: True. To run, your foot pushes back on the ground. Friction stops the foot sliding, so the ground can push you forward. With little friction, your foot slides back instead.

items.p: Label the three pictures of a ball landing on a pillow: 'falling', 'pillow squashes', 'ball stops'.
items.why: The ball falls, the pillow squashes instead of the ball, and the ball stops, because the pillow springs back too slowly to push it up.
items.art: Three small pictures in a row: a ball above a pillow, a ball pressing into a pillow, and a ball resting in a dent in the pillow, each with a blank label.

items.p: Kavya's tennis ball bounced to 55 cm on the floor. She left it in the fridge for an hour and dropped it again. It bounced to 48 cm. What is the best next step?
opts: Do it 3 times cold and 3 times warm before deciding
Say cold balls always bounce lower
Give up, because it went wrong
items.why: One try can be a fluke. Testing 3 times each way shows whether the difference is real. Many balls do bounce a little lower when cold, but a scientist checks before deciding.

items.p: A kangaroo needs to travel far across dry land to find food and water. How do the long tendons in their legs help them?
items.a: With each hop, the tendons in the kangaroo's legs stretch as they land, then spring back and help lift them into the next hop. So they can hop a long way without tiring as fast.
items.why: A strong answer starts with the kangaroo's problem, travelling far, and says how springy tendons help solve it.

items.p: Your ball bounced to about 55 cm on the floor and about 5 cm on the pillow. Write a short rule that explains both results, and test your rule on one new surface.
items.a: A strong rule: the softer a surface is, and the slower it springs back, the lower the bounce. It names a new surface, such as a bed or a carpet, makes a guess, tests it, and says if the rule worked.
items.why: A strong answer makes a general rule from evidence and then checks it, which is what scientists do.

items.p: Three people explain why a footballer's spinning kick curves in the air.

views.says: The spinning ball drags air round with it and throws it to one side. So the air pushes the ball the other way.
The air moves faster on one side of the spinning ball. Faster air presses less, so the ball is pushed to that side.

items.ask: Which explanation is clearer to you? Explain it in your own words. Then say whether the two could both be right.
items.a: A strong answer explains one view in its own words, for example that the ball pushes air one way so the air pushes the ball the other way. It sees that both describe the same curve, and that both can be true at once.
items.why: Scientists agree that a spinning ball curves, the Magnus effect. Teachers argue about which explanation is clearer. Both are correct ways of describing it.

items.p: Without any air, at which angle would a ball thrown at the same speed go furthest?
opts: 45 degrees, halfway between flat and straight up
items.why: Thrown flat, the ball soon hits the ground. Thrown straight up, it comes back to you. Halfway, 45 degrees, gives the best mix of going forward and staying up. In real sport, with air and the thrower's height, the best angle is a little lower.

items.p: Draw three throws from the same hand at the same speed: nearly flat, halfway up, and nearly straight up. Show where each lands.
items.a: The nearly flat throw lands close. The nearly straight up throw goes high and lands close. The halfway throw lands furthest away.
items.why: This shows why the angle of a throw matters as much as its speed.
items.art: A stick figure on the left side of a blank page, with a flat ground line.

items.p: Revathi says, 'A trampoline is soft like a pillow, so it should give a low bounce too.' Explain what she is missing.
items.a: A trampoline is soft, but it is also elastic. It springs back fast, while the ball is still touching it, so it pushes the ball up. A pillow springs back too slowly. So being soft is not enough to lose a bounce. What matters is how fast the surface springs back.
items.why: A strong answer separates 'soft' from 'springs back slowly', which is the key idea of the unit.

items.p: Tennis has a rule for how bouncy a ball must be: dropped from 254 cm onto concrete, it must bounce back to between 135 and 147 cm.
items.why: True. Tennis balls are tested by dropping them onto concrete. A ball that bounces too high or too low is not allowed. That is about half the height it fell from.

items.p: A cricket ball and a rubber ball are dropped from the same height onto wet mud. What will happen?
opts: Both will hardly bounce, because the mud squashes
The cricket ball will bounce higher, because it is heavier
items.why: Wet mud squashes and stays squashed, so it takes the bounce from any ball. The ball's weight doesn't change that.

items.p: In Galileo's Table, Aparna's marbles landed 30 cm, 42 cm and 58 cm from the table. Her friend says the marble falls straight down for a while, then moves forward. Use Aparna's results to show why that is wrong.
items.a: If the marble fell straight down first, it would land close to the table each time. But it landed further away when it was faster, so it was moving forward the whole time it fell. Its path was a curve, starting at the table edge.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence, the landing distances, to test someone else's idea.

items: a camel's wide, padded feet
Soft ground

items.why: Wide feet spread an animal's weight so they sink less on soft ground. Hard hooves grip and don't wear away on firm ground and rock. A strong answer starts with the animal's problem: sinking, or slipping.

items.p: Put these surfaces in order, from the one that gives a ball the highest bounce to the lowest.
items: a pillow
a doormat
a stone floor
a plate of dry rice
items.why: The harder the surface, and the less it gives way, the higher the bounce. Rice grains slide apart and don't spring back at all.

items.p: An athletics track is made of firm rubber, not hard concrete and not soft sand. Why do you think it is made that way?
items.a: It is firm, so the runner's push comes back to them and they can run fast. It is a little soft and springy, so landing is gentler on the runner's legs than on concrete. It also grips their shoes, so they don't slip.
items.why: A strong answer weighs two needs: a firm push back for speed, and a little give for safety.

items.p: Nila stands on a scale in her house. She bends her knees and jumps up. Just as she pushes off, what does the scale show?
opts: More than her weight, because she pushes down harder
items.why: To jump up, she must push down on the scale harder than her weight. The scale pushes back up just as hard, and that extra push lifts her. Once she is in the air, it reads zero.

items.p: Label the forces on a runner: the runner's weight, the ground pushing up, and the ground pushing forward.
items.why: Gravity pulls the runner down. The ground pushes up so they don't sink, and pushes forward because their foot pushes back on it. A strong answer draws the arrows in the right directions.
items.art: A side view of a runner with one foot on the ground, with three blank arrows.

items.p: A squash ball bounces higher once it has been hit against the wall for a few minutes. Why do you think players warm it up first?
items.a: A warm squash ball is more elastic and springs back better, so it bounces higher. A cold squash ball hardly bounces, so the game would be slow.
items.why: A strong answer links the warming to a better bounce. It may also notice that the warmth comes from the energy of the hits.

items.p: The strong, stretchy cord that joins a muscle to a bone, and springs back when you run, is called a ____.
items.why: Tendons stretch as your foot lands and spring back as you push off. The Achilles tendon at the back of your heel is the biggest in the body.

items.p: Design a shoe for running on a beach. Draw it and label two features that help on soft sand.
items.a: A drawing with features such as a wide sole so the foot sinks less, or a grippy bottom so the sand doesn't slide away. Each feature is labelled with what it does.
items.why: A strong answer starts from the problem of soft sand, sinking and sliding, and gives a feature for each.

open_questions.q: Does training on sand make a runner faster on a track?
open_questions.why_open: Sand training clearly works the legs harder. But studies have been small and do not agree on whether it improves speed on a hard track.

open_questions.q: What is the best floor for a running track?
open_questions.why_open: Tracks that are a little springy seem to help runners, but how springy is best for speed, and for avoiding injuries, is still studied.

open_questions.q: Is barefoot running safer than running in shoes?
open_questions.why_open: Barefoot runners land differently, which some think is gentler. There is not yet enough evidence either way about injuries.

open_questions.q: Exactly how much do the tendons and the muscles each do in a running stride?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure the forces, but it is hard to see inside a living leg while it runs. The share changes with speed and with the ground.

maths.problem: In the bounce test, Kavya's ball bounced to 55 cm on the floor, 40 cm on the doormat, 20 cm on the folded bedsheet, 5 cm on the pillow and 0 cm on the rice. Draw a bar chart. Which surface gave the highest bounce, and how much higher was it than the doormat?
maths.answer: The floor gave the highest bounce. It was 15 cm higher than the doormat.
maths.explain: The floor's bar is tallest, at 55 cm. The doormat's is 40 cm. 55 minus 40 is 15. So the floor bounce was 15 cm higher.
maths.context: This is about the bounce test. You drop one ball from 100 cm onto five surfaces and measure each bounce.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which surface gave the best bounce, and how the bounce falls as the surface gets softer.

maths.problem: Kavya dropped the ball from 100 cm and it bounced to 55 cm on the floor. Then she dropped it from 50 cm. Predict how high it will bounce, and say why.
maths.answer: About 27 or 28 cm, roughly half of 55.
maths.explain: From 100 cm it came back about 55 cm, just over half. On the same floor, the ball gives back about the same share of the fall. Half of 100 is 50, so half of 55 is about 27 or 28 cm. A real ball may differ a little, so test it.
maths.context: This is about the bounce test on the bare floor. It asks you to predict a bounce from a lower height.
maths.why_maths: Seeing that the bounce is about half the drop lets you predict a new result before you test it.

maths.problem: Meenakshi throws a ball three times at the same speed: at an angle of 15 degrees, 45 degrees and 75 degrees. Without air, the 15 and 75 degree throws land in the same place. Which throw lands furthest? What do 15 and 75 add up to?
maths.answer: The 45 degree throw lands furthest. 15 and 75 add up to 90.
maths.explain: Without air, the throw halfway up, at 45 degrees, goes furthest. Two angles that add up to 90 degrees, such as 15 and 75, land in the same place: the low one goes fast and flat, and the high one goes up and comes down. 15 + 75 = 90.
maths.context: This is about throwing. An angle says how much a throw is tilted up from the flat ground.

maths.problem: In the arm swing test, Nithya jumped 92, 98 and 95 cm with her arms behind her back, and 110, 116 and 112 cm with her arms swinging. Find each middle number. How much further did swinging her arms take her?
maths.answer: 95 cm and 112 cm. Swinging her arms took her 17 cm further.
maths.explain: In order, 92, 95, 98 gives a middle of 95. In order, 110, 112, 116 gives a middle of 112. 112 minus 95 is 17. So she jumped 17 cm further with her arms.
maths.context: This is about the arm swing test, where you jump from standing with and without swinging your arms.
maths.why_maths: The middle number is fair to both ways of jumping. Taking one from the other tells us exactly how much the arms helped.

roots.context: We have learned how a ball bounces, and how the ground changes a bounce and a run. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your ball bounced high off the hard floor, but hardly at all off a pillow. On the floor, the ball squashed and sprang back up. On the pillow, the pillow squashed instead, and sprang back too slowly to push. Soft sand does the same to a runner's feet, so every step on sand takes more work.
deep_truth.habit: We think of the ground as something that just lies there while the ball or the runner does all the work. But a bounce and a stride are made by two things together. What the ground does when it is squashed decides how much of the push comes back.
deep_truth.evidence: One ball, dropped from the same height, bounced to about 55 cm off the floor and about 5 cm off a pillow. Only the surface changed. Jogging on a mattress felt harder than on the floor, for the same reason.

three.who_am_i: You are a springy body. Your tendons stretch and spring back every time you land.
three.what_is_life: Kangaroos, camels and runners have bodies shaped for the ground they move on.
three.what_is_this_world: The ground is never just still. Every floor squashes a tiny bit and pushes back on you.

roots.thread: A ball on its own cannot bounce, and a runner on their own cannot run. Each bounce and each step is made between two things that push on each other. A hard floor and a soft pillow meet the same ball, and two different bounces come out. So a game is not something one player does alone. It happens between the player, the ball and the ground, all pushing at once.

teachings.teaching: Two bundles of reeds can stand up by leaning on each other. Take one away, and the other falls.
teachings.link: A bounce needs the ball and the ground together. Take away a firm ground, as on a pillow or soft sand, and the bounce falls flat.

teachings.source: Jain anekantavada, the story of the blind men and the elephant

teachings.link: The same ball seems bouncy on the floor and dead on the pillow. To understand a bounce, you have to look at the ball and the ground together.

science.text: Every push comes with an equal push back. When your foot pushes the ground, the ground pushes your foot just as hard. This is Newton's third law.
Tendons in the legs store energy as they stretch when a foot lands, and return much of it in the next step. This is part of why running on firm ground costs less energy than on sand.

other_view.view: A bounce is just the ball's own elasticity meeting a floor. The ground is a surface, and the skill is in the player. Talking about the ground 'taking part' adds nothing to the physics.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home in a flat, with the listed materials. The bounce test needs a hard floor and a wall or door for the paper ruler. Reading a bounce by eye is hard, so the steps suggest a helper crouching at eye level and a slow-motion phone video. A folded sheet adds a few centimetres of height, so the step says to measure from its top. On the pillow and the rice the ball may not lift at all, and the step says this is a real result. Galileo's Table uses a flat gap of table after the ramp, so the marble leaves the edge moving flat, and a plate of rava to show where it lands. The arm swing test is done barefoot on a dry floor with a grown-up watching. The water jet and the water balloons are done in the bathroom or on a balcony. The jog on a mattress uses a mattress on the floor, never a bed. Both games work in a living room. The spine fits about 80 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: For hundreds of years, many scholars in Europe taught that a thrown ball or a cannonball moves in a straight line until the force of the throw runs out. Then it falls straight down. Books showed cannonballs flying along a straight line and then dropping, like a hook. Niccolò Tartaglia, an Italian mathematician, disagreed. As a boy he had been badly wounded by a soldier's sword, and it left him with a stammer. His nickname, Tartaglia, means 'the stammerer'. His family was too poor to keep him at school, so he taught himself. In 1537 he wrote a book about the paths of cannonballs. He showed that aiming halfway up, at 45 degrees, sends a cannonball furthest. He also argued that no part of the path is really straight, because the ball's weight pulls on it all the time. About 70 years later, Galileo Galilei tested this. He rolled balls down a ramp and off a table, and marked where they landed. Faster balls landed further away, and the numbers fitted a curve. In 1638 he showed that, without air, a thrown thing follows a smooth curve called a parabola.
how_we_found_out.who: Niccolò Tartaglia, an Italian mathematician, and Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist
how_we_found_out.when: 1537 (Tartaglia's first book on cannonballs) to 1638 (Galileo's book Two New Sciences)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought a thrown ball flies straight until the push of the throw is used up, and then drops straight down. Tartaglia argued that the path curves all the way. Galileo's experiments with balls rolled off a table showed it, and he proved the curve is a parabola.
